qs.q: Which cellular organelle is the primary site for generating energy via oxidative phosphorylation and is therefore the earliest to be affected during acute hypoxic cell injury?
o: Rough endoplasmic reticulum, which processes newly synthesized proteins
Mitochondria, which generate energy via oxidative phosphorylation
Lysosomes, which contain digestive enzymes to degrade cellular waste
Golgi apparatus, which modifies and packages cellular proteins
qs.e: Mitochondria generate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation, making them the first organelle to fail when oxygen supply is halted. Other organelles like the rough endoplasmic reticulum are affected secondarily as ATP becomes depleted.

qs.q: A patient experiences subacute bilateral loss of central vision due to an inherited defect in oxidative phosphorylation enzymes. Molecular analysis confirms a point mutation in mitochondrial DNA. What condition does this represent?
qs.e: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by mutations in mitochondrial genes encoding oxidative phosphorylation enzymes. Duchenne muscular dystrophy and Huntington disease are nuclear DNA disorders.

qs.q: What is the primary site of oxidative phosphorylation in eukaryotic cells?
qs.e: In eukaryotes, oxidative phosphorylation occurs across the inner mitochondrial membrane where electron transport creates a proton gradient. Prokaryotes utilize their plasma membrane for this process instead.

qs.q: What is the primary function of the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation in aerobic respiration?
o: Generating a proton gradient used by ATP synthase for high ATP yield
Fixing carbon dioxide into glucose utilizing light-dependent reactions
Regenerating NAD+ from NADH via an endogenous organic molecule
Fermenting pyruvate into lactic acid under strict anaerobic conditions
qs.e: Oxidative phosphorylation uses an electron transport chain to create a proton gradient across the membrane, which ATP synthase then uses to generate a high yield of ATP. Fermentation and substrate-level phosphorylation yield much lower amounts of ATP without relying on an external electron transport chain.

qs.q: An insecticide disrupting the NADH enzyme of the oxidative phosphorylation pathway is applied to an insect breeding site. Which chemical matches this description?
qs.e: Rotenone targets the NADH enzyme of the oxidative phosphorylation pathway. Propoxur targets acetylcholinesterase, while deltamethrin acts on sodium channels.

qs.q: A histology student observes cellular organelles under transmission electron microscopy. Organelle A shows inner folds called cristae and is responsible for ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation. What is organelle A?
qs.e: Mitochondria are responsible for ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation and house the citric acid cycle. The Golgi apparatus is involved in protein modification and sorting, not primary ATP generation.

qs.q: Cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect produce how many ATP molecules per glucose compared to normal oxidative phosphorylation?
qs.e: ** Aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect) produces only 2 ATP molecules per glucose molecule, versus 36 from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Despite being less efficient, this metabolic shift allows rapid cell division by shunting glucose carbons toward biosynthetic pathways.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Oxidative phosphorylation is the mitochondrial process that couples electron transport to ATP synthesis, essential for cellular energy. Clinicians must recognize its failure in mitochondrial disorders, sepsis, and drug toxicity.

sections.p: Oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the electron transport chain (ETC) pumps protons to create a gradient that drives ATP synthase.
Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ travel through complexes I–IV, releasing energy to pump protons. The resulting electrochemical gradient powers ATP synthase (complex V).

t.b: Measures oxygen consumption to assess ETC function; low rates suggest complex deficiency.
Detects assembly defects of ETC complexes; abnormal bands indicate specific complex mutations.
Elevated lactate indicates impaired oxidative phosphorylation and anaerobic metabolism.

sections.p: ATP/ADP ratio, pH, and reactive oxygen species modulate ETC activity. Uncouplers like DCCD inhibit proton pumping, reducing ATP synthesis.
Genetic mutations in mtDNA or nuclear genes encoding ETC proteins cause mitochondrial myopathies, cardiomyopathies, and neurodegenerative diseases.

t.b: Shows reduced cytochrome c oxidase activity; confirms complex IV deficiency.
Identifies nuclear gene mutations affecting ETC proteins.

sections.p: Sepsis, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and certain drugs (e.g., metformin, cyanide) impair OxPhos, leading to organ failure.

t.b: High levels predict risk of lactic acidosis; guide discontinuation.
Low pH and high lactate indicate impaired oxidative metabolism.

sections.p: Remember the P/O ratio (ATP per oxygen) and that complex I mutations often present with exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Cardiogenic shock due to mitochondrial cardiomyopathy

faq.q: Why does metformin cause lactic acidosis?
faq.a: It inhibits complex I, reducing oxidative phosphorylation and increasing anaerobic glycolysis.

faq.q: What is the difference between complex I and complex IV deficiencies?
faq.a: Complex I causes early-onset neurodegeneration; complex IV often presents with cardiomyopathy and exercise intolerance.
They may reduce oxidative stress but do not correct the underlying ETC defect.
